TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
THURSDAY, 15 DECEMBER 2022 AT 9.58 AM (AEST)
DAY 21
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Counsel Assisting
MS RENEE BERRY, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR A. VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: I will just take appearances for the day.
MR SCOTT: May it please, Commissioner, I appear with Ms Berry for today's evidence.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Ms Hogan-Doran.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission, I appear today with Mr Vial for the
Commonwealth.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. And, look, I will just put it on the record, Ms
Hogan-Doran, that you and I exchanged pleasantries at the Bar Association dinner for the
new silks last night.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: We did, in the company of others.
COMMISSIONER: Yes.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Before the evidence commences with the first witness, Commissioner, I seek to
tender the exhibits for today's evidence as per the list, which I understand has been provided
to you by your associate, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. So all of the exhibits going in now?
MR SCOTT: Yes. If it pleases.
COMMISSIONER: 2689 to 2807?
MR SCOTT: That's so.
COMMISSIONER: Right. They're admitted as exhibits with the numbers they bear in the list.
<EXHIBITS 2689 TO 2807 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. Now, we've got Ms Harfield?
MR SCOTT: Yes, I call her.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. Ms Harfield, would you rather take an oath or an affirmation?
MS HARFIELD: I would like to affirm.

<KAREN MARY HARFIELD, AFFIRMED
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT
COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Ms Harfield, could you please tell the Commission
your full name?
MS HARFIELD: Karen Mary Harfield.
MR SCOTT: And you received a Notice to yourself from the Commission dated 20 October
2022 requiring that you provide a Statement and produce documents. Do you recall that?
MS HARFIELD: I was actually overseas on that date, but once I returned from overseas I did
get the Notice, yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And you produced a Statement in response to that Notice dated 4
December 2022?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: Is the contents of that Statement true and correct to the best of your knowledge
and belief?
MS HARFIELD: It is.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. You've got some documents there with you, Ms Harfield; that's right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And I understand - and correct me if I'm wrong - that those documents generally
constitute the various exhibits that relate to your evidence?
MS HARFIELD: So some of the documents were provided to me this morning, and I don't
necessarily go specifically to those in my Statement. But the ones in my Statement are also
there.
MR SCOTT: Okay. But they constitute the various exhibits that, as I understand it, have been
tendered for the purpose of your evidence; is that right? Thank you. And you've got another
document there, I understand, which is a timeline of your various roles within the
Department of Human Services; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, just because I did a number of different roles and there were a number of
sort of iterations. So it's just really to try and get my thoughts in a logical order.

MR SCOTT: An aide-memoire, if you will?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. You are currently the General Manager in the Enterprise
Portfolio Management Office of what is now known as Services Australia; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: That's right.
MR SCOTT: The Department formally known as the Department of Human Services?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And you've held that position since 25 October 2022?
MS HARFIELD: No, I think July '21, actually.
MR SCOTT: My notes. Thank you. But previously you occupied the role of General Manager
of the Customer Compliance Division of the Department of Human Services between 14
March 2016 and 30 April 2017; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: And to be clear, within that period, there was a period that you went on leave
between 16 February 2017 and 26 March 2017; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. You joined the Department of Human Services on 14 March 2016?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: And prior to that date, the equivalent role within Customer Compliance was
carried out within the Business Integrity Division under Mark Withnell; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, it was just one division.
MR SCOTT: Okay. From the point that you commenced in your role in the Department of
Human Services - is this right - Mr Withnell was, and continued to be, the Senior Responsible
Officer for the Strengthening the Integrity of Welfare Payments Budget Measure; is that
right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: The term "Senior Responsible Officer", does that have a particular meaning?

MS HARFIELD: So within sort of project management discipline, it would be the sort of
person that is managing most of the aspects of the project. So if there's a technical build,
business requirements, design, user specification, the Senior Responsible Officer is there to
pull all of those elements together. And you might have several project managers that are
responsible for the other sort of specific sort of specialist areas. And depending on the size of
a program, you then might have a Program Sponsor as well. But Senior Responsible Officer is
really the sort of main architect of the whole program.
MR SCOTT: Can you tell us for how long Mr Withnell continued in the role of Senior
Responsible Officer for that Budget Measure?
MS HARFIELD: So for the Budget Measure itself - so Strengthening the Integrity of Welfare
Payments had a number of different projects that made up a program. One of those
elements was income data matching and the build of the Online Compliance system. I can't
be accurate about a specific date. But really, in terms of the measure, that was going on for a
sort of number of years. But it was really, I suppose, focused on the build of the Online
Compliance system. But he was the ongoing SRO for Strengthening the Integrity of Welfare
Payments until it ended, but I can't tell you what date that was.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And so when you say, "ongoing Senior Responsible Officer for the
Strengthening the Integrity of Welfare Payments", does that mean he had that responsibility
with respect to the build of the Online Compliance Intervention?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And did he continue in that role at least until early 2017, to your memory?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, I would say that that was - I would say that was right.
MR SCOTT: And - so within the Strengthening the Integrity of Welfare Payments Budget
Measure - would this be right - that included the Scheme that became what is now known as
Robodebt?
MS HARFIELD: So it included an element of that. So the Budget Measures - there were a
number of Budget Measures from, I think, the 2015-16 Budget. There was also a number of
measures from the MYEFO period, so the mid-year economic period, and each of those
measures were going to use the Online Compliance system. And so together they make up
what is known as Robodebt.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Can you give evidence to the Commission as to the extent of Mr Withnell's
involvement in the Robodebt Scheme during the period that you were General Manager of
Customer Compliance?
MS HARFIELD: So certainly when I first arrived, the Budget Measure in relation to income
matching had already commenced. There had been a - there was sort of a number of phases.
So there had been an ongoing pilot. So when I went - I was briefed on these issues by Mark

Division. And the - there had been a pilot process, which was a sort of - known commonly
within the Department as a sort of rapid response. So it was a sort of halfway measure
before the Online Compliance system went into production, and that had been going since - I
understand, since the July of 2015. And during that financial year, the build of the Online
Compliance system was progressing. So the user specifications, the business requirements,
had been done and established, and the technical build was in progress when I arrived.
MR SCOTT: So you referred to some briefings from Mr Withnell and Mr Britton when you
started. So that was in March 2016?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. So there - and Jason Ryman as well, who was the Director of - within
Customer Compliance, which really was giving me the background on the Budget Measures
and the requirements and where it was up to and a sort of, you know, situation view of
where the program was up to. Along with, obviously, all of the other work that the Customer
Compliance Division needed to do across that year.
MR SCOTT: And from that point on until early 2017, did you continue to have dealings with
Mr Withnell in relation to the - what was first the manual intervention that you describe in
your evidence and then later the Online Compliance Intervention?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Thank you. If we could just bring up on the screen paragraph 110 of your
Statement on page 30. Call that paragraph out, please. You refer to briefings by Mr Lumley in
that paragraph. Do you see that?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Can you tell us when those briefings occurred?
MS HARFIELD: So that would have been when I sort of first - I don't know exact dates, but
certainly, you know, I had a number of introductory meetings and briefings with the
directors. So Mr Lumley being one of the directors in Customer Compliance. And there was,
obviously, quite a focus on the Online Compliance system because of the requirements
around the Budget Measures.
MR SCOTT: So around March 2016?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, yes. Yes, across a sort of couple of weeks, you know, in sort of hour slots
or whatever it happened to be, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I just want to ask you about the last sentence in that paragraph:
To the best of my recollection I was not informed or aware of any changes to raising debts
connected to the increased use of automation by DHS.

Can I just clarify: are you saying that you were not told anything about any changes to the
raising of debts connected to the increased use of automation or are you saying that that, in
fact, you were positively told that there had not been any change?
MS HARFIELD: So my understanding from the briefings was that the difference between
what had happened previously to what the online system was going to do was that it
was - the online system was there to encourage people to go online and manage the - any
discrepancy or potential overpayment using the online system, and that that was the
difference.
COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask you: when Mr Britton and Mr Withnell and Mr Ryman briefed
you, did they explain what the manual compliance pilot involved?
MS HARFIELD: I don't - I don't remember it in particular detail, but I do know that that
was - that was what was still happening at that time when I joined.
COMMISSIONER: You don't recall them telling you that it involved a customer being
presented with the ATO data and invited to correct it, and if they didn't, the data would be
applied?
MS HARFIELD: Yes - no, no. That was part of the briefing, yes.
COMMISSIONER: And also if the customer did not respond, the ATO data would be applied in
an averaged form?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And this may seem an odd question, but was Mr Withnell part of that
briefing?
MS HARFIELD: I had quite a lot of conversations and briefings from Mark Withnell, yes.
COMMISSIONER: In which he no doubt referred to the actual process involved at stages; I
assume?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. I mean, it was like a sort of - an introduction into, I suppose, the
development of the Budget Measures.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thanks. Thanks.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. At paragraph 121 of your Statement on page 31, you
refer to what you describe as five iterations of the Robodebt Scheme. And you mentioned
already the Pilot Program, which operated at a time that you weren't at the Department. You
referred then to the Manual Compliance Intervention Program. And the point you make is
that by the time you joined the Department on 14 March 2016, that was towards the end of
that iteration of the Scheme. And then you refer to the Online Compliance Intervention, also

known as OCI. You state that was deployed in July 2016 with initially 1000 compliance
reviews initiated. Do you see that?
MS HARFIELD: I do.
MR SCOTT: And that was - is this right - before the Scheme went fully live in September 2016;
is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: It was sort of a testing of the online system?
MS HARFIELD: There was a - well, what was called a staged implementation, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what's a staged implementation?
MS HARFIELD: Well, it was - so with the system itself - so when I arrived, the build was
behind time and over budget. And even though it was supposed to go into sort of full
deployment on 1 July, it wasn't ready for that to occur. The system itself went into
production on 11 July, and that was where the staged implementation was applied. So rather
than the system being switched on and allowed to run end to end with the process, that
reviews were initiated through the system but then physically checked to make sure that
they were correct before then going to the customer. But once the system went completely
live, that check bit didn't happen.
MR SCOTT: In terms of the checking in this initial phase involving 1,000 intervention, who
was doing the checking?
MS HARFIELD: So they would be Compliance Officers.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And by "checking", what are you describing?
MS HARFIELD: So by checking, it's making sure that the letter that the system produced,
which was the notification to the customer, was correct.
MR SCOTT: Right. And that letter essentially would tell a customer that there's a difference
between what the - I should say social security recipient had declared to Centrelink and what
had been declared about their income to the Australian Taxation Office?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. So it was asking the customer to go online and confirm or provide more
information in relation to that data that was presented in the letter.
MR SCOTT: And - so that would mean, in terms of checking the correctness of the letter,
checking to ensure that what was said in the letter about what had been declared about
their income to the ATO was, in fact - had been declared about their income to the ATO; is
that right?

MS HARFIELD: Or whether they had, you know, other information.
MR SCOTT: Okay. When you say, "whether they had other information", do you mean other
information on the file?
MS HARFIELD: No, no. The customer.
MR SCOTT: I see.
MS HARFIELD: Correct - could - you know, had a - so in terms of the system - so the customer
online can see the payments and then they could correct - if those - if that wasn't correct in
relation to them as an individual, they could change that data.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And what were Compliance Officers checking in relation to that?
MS HARFIELD: So in terms of the stage and implementation?
MR SCOTT: Yes.
MS HARFIELD: So what they were checking was that the letter was going to the correct
customer and that the data that we - you were asking that customer to check was the data.
So that the system was compiling that correctly for that customer to look at.
MR SCOTT: Right. And by "data", you're referring to the ATO data?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned that at this time of the staged implementation,
the program was behind schedule and over budget. Can you say whether there was any
pressure that you felt to accelerate the implementation of the program?
MS HARFIELD: So there was a very, very strong focus on the achievement of the Budget
Measures, particularly from the Deputy Secretary, almost sort of daily sort of interaction
about where the system was up to, when the system would go live. As I say, it had been
anticipated that it would go live on 1 July, which it didn't do. So I would say sort of when I
first joined the Department, Mark as the SRO - that sort of would have been more of his
focus, and I was focused more predominantly on a sort of broader range of compliance
activities. But by the July, the focus was very much on the Budget Measures and delivery
around them.
MR SCOTT: Okay. I'm going to ask you about the Manual Compliance Intervention Program,
which you provide a description of at paragraph 126 on page 32 of your Statement. If we can
bring that up, please. I'm really interested in subparagraph (a). If we could highlight that,
please. Can you see that subparagraph (a) there, Ms Harfield?
MS HARFIELD: I can.

MR SCOTT: Thank you. You make this point in relation to the Manual Compliance
Intervention program, that:
…apart from the Pilot Program, this was the first time ATO PAYG data was used as the main
methodology to calculate the total amount of income earned by the customer from
employment during the relevant period of employment and multiplying that amount by the
percentage of time that the customer received income support payments during the review
period.
And you say:
However, I was not aware of this at the time.
I just want to clarify some aspects of this Statement so that we're clear in understanding
what you're saying. So, firstly, when we're talking about the ATO PAYG data, that's data as to
income received from the ATO in respect of the relevant social security recipients; correct?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And that data wouldn't be data as to actual income earned per fortnight by the
customer; correct?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Typically, although not necessarily always, it would be for an entire period - sorry,
an entire year over which the customer earned income; correct?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Sometimes it might be for a shorter period; is that correct?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. I believe so, yes.
MR SCOTT: But never did it specify actual amounts earned per fortnight?
MS HARFIELD: No.
MR SCOTT: And you state:
This was the first time that data was used as the main methodology to calculate the total
amount earned.
Do you see that, in that paragraph?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.

MR SCOTT: And by that - would this be right - you're saying that this was the first time that
ATO data was used to calculate what had been earned per fortnight using what is known as
income averaging; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: In terms of it being the initiation of a compliance review, yes.
MR SCOTT: Right.
COMMISSIONER: What the Statement does say is it's the first time it was used as the main
methodology.
MR SCOTT: Yes. And so in terms of the words "main methodology", is that distinguishing
from another method to calculate actual income without first going to the ATO data to
calculate that income? Is that what you're saying, Ms Harfield?
MS HARFIELD: No, I think the difference is that previously a Compliance Officer would do a
sort of end-to-end process in relation to a compliance review, whereas this methodology
initiated a request to the customer based on the ATO data. So that was the comparison.
MR SCOTT: So by "end-to-end process by a Compliance Officer", are you referring to the
previous process whereby before a customer was contacted or attempted to be contacted
for the purpose of a review, a Compliance Officer would actually review the whole file held in
relation to the customer to ascertain whether there was a discrepancy between what had
been declared to the ATO and what had actually been declared by the customer; is that
right?
MS HARFIELD: I don't know that I can say it was that exactly. I'm not a - I wasn't a Compliance
Officer. But as I understood it at the time - or understand it now, was that customers would
be contacted in relation to compliance reviews and then a Compliance Officer would find the
information, whereas this process was saying to the customer, "There is a difference
between what we have got on a record in terms of the Department and what we have been
told by the - matched with the ATO data, and we want you to go online and check that.”
MR SCOTT: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Can I check this with you, though. You said in your evidence just now that
this was the first time the ATO data had been used to initiate a review. What you actually say
in your Statement is that it's the first time it was used as the main methodology to calculate
the total amount of income earned, which indicates that it's actually used for the first time as
the main methodology of arriving at an income figure, not just initiating a review.
MS HARFIELD: So my understanding was that the information for the customer in the
Department was then matched against the record from the ATO. And based on a number of
criteria, that was the trigger to initiate the review. And I'm not quite sure -
COMMISSIONER: Okay. But there was nothing new about that, was there, the comparison

MS HARFIELD: No, no, no.
COMMISSIONER: Right.
MS HARFIELD: But the methodology to then go out and ask the customer to go online to
confirm or update.
COMMISSIONER: But, Ms Harfield, that's not just what I'm reading in your Statement. It says:
This is the first time ATO PAYG data was used as the main methodology to calculate the total
amount of income earned.
Not just about how the customer was asked to respond. And I suspect that would be
accurate, wouldn't it, that it was the first time? Anyway. What do you say about -
MS HARFIELD: I'm not sure I can clarify it any further for you. I'm sorry.
COMMISSIONER: Well, your Statement is correct, I assume, when it says it's the first time it
was used as the main methodology to calculate the total amount of income earned?
MS HARFIELD: Well, I understood that it was the first time that it was used in terms of the
volume for the matching. But I appreciate that's not what that sentence says.
COMMISSIONER: Why did you say it? Is it possibly because it was right?
MS HARFIELD: I - no, I don't - I don't know. I can't tell you the difference between the two.
COMMISSIONER: The difference is evident; it's whether it's initiating a particular form of
review or whether it's actually used to calculate a debt - the - the income and then, in due
course, the debt.
MS HARFIELD: Yes. So it certainly - so it certainly was used if the customer didn't engage in
the process, yes.
COMMISSIONER: Yes. But what you're saying there is this is the first time that that was used
as the main way of proceeding.
MS HARFIELD: That - yes.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thanks.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. And by "main way of proceeding", that's to distinguish
from a situation that had occurred in the past whereby averaging might only be used
relatively rarely because the Compliance Officer has undertaken a number of inquiries with
the customer, an employer; reviewed the file to ascertain whether or not there is, in fact, a

relevant discrepancy; and used those other sources of information as the primary
methodology to calculate the customer's income. Do you understand the distinction?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, yes. So I think - in terms of the use of averaging, I think when the - the
way the system was described to me, there was a sense that the initiation would - that
people would engage with the process and, therefore, the number of times averaging would
need to be used would be less. But that is not what eventuated.
MR SCOTT: But what I'm just trying to get you clear on, Ms Harfield, is what you understood
to be the main methodology - sorry, I will start this again - what you now understand was the
main methodology for calculating the total amount of income earned by a customer prior to
Robodebt. Do you understand my question?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And do you accept that prior to Robodebt, income averaging was not the
main methodology for calculating how much income?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And will you agree with us that - and it's consistent with what you say in
your Statement – that, apart from the Pilot Program, the manual intervention was the first
time that averaging was used to calculate - sorry, used as the main methodology to calculate
a customer's income. Do you agree with that?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. In the last sentence of that paragraph, you say:
I was not aware of this at the time.
What time are you referring to when you say, "at the time"?
MS HARFIELD: So I think when I first started, in terms of the sense of the Budget Measure
itself, the way it was described and briefed to me was this - I think one of the assumptions
that was in the program of work was that most people would engage with the process.
MR SCOTT: So when you say you were not aware of this at the time - so firstly, when you say,
"the time", you're referring to that period in about March 2016 when you were receiving
briefings; is that right?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And am I understanding you to be saying that when the words "I was not aware
of this at that time" - what is the "this" in that sentence that you're referring to that you
weren't aware of?

MS HARFIELD: Well, what I think subsequently, you know, eventuated was that customers
either didn't respond to a letter, if they got a letter, or - or they didn't respond to a
notification in their myGov account. And so the process itself continued on using the ATO
data on more occasions than had been anticipated in the program of work.
MR SCOTT: Right. So what you're saying you weren't aware of is that, in the program, the use
of the ATO data as the main methodology to calculate the total amount of income in that
program as it went on - that's what you weren't aware of. Is that what you're saying?
MS HARFIELD: That, yes, the number of times the requirement for averaging would be used -
MR SCOTT: I see.
MS HARFIELD: - was a lot more significant that had been described originally.
MR SCOTT: I see.
COMMISSIONER: But it had never been used as the default mechanism for calculating debt,
had it? It had never been automatically applied to a customer record.
MS HARFIELD: So my understanding in terms of not automatically applied, no, because you
would have engaged with a Compliance Officer, but that ATO data had been used to average
previously.
COMMISSIONER: And what was your understanding of how often that had occurred or in
what circumstances?
MS HARFIELD: Well, it wasn't - and it was described in the program similarly, that it would be
used as a sort of end resort. You know, it was only used where you couldn't get other
information.
COMMISSIONER: Where was it described as that?
MS HARFIELD: Well, that was really in my sort of interactions and briefings and also in the
written documentation.
COMMISSIONER: Which written documentation?
MS HARFIELD: The sort of presentational briefing documents that Mr Withnell and
Mr Britton went through with me.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. And just so I can understand this, they explained to you it had been
used as a last resort in the past and would be used as a last resort in this program?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.

COMMISSIONER: Alright. But it became pretty clear, presumably, pretty fast, that it wasn't
being used as a last resort; it was being used as the default position?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: And when did you realise that?
MS HARFIELD: Well, I would say that that started to emerge when, in the September, Deputy
Secretary Malisa Golightly asked for an increase in the number of reviews that were initiated
to get us back on to - in her mind, back on track for the volume of reviews that were required
to meet the Budget Measure.
COMMISSIONER: So September 2016.
MS HARFIELD: Yes, September 2016. And then as a result of those increased volumes of
reviews that had been initiated, there were a number of system issues, there were a number
of, you know, customer - the sort of level of customer dissatisfaction with the process itself
started to emerge, and it started to become clearer that customers were only engaging with
the process when they got a debt letter. So -
COMMISSIONER: So -
MS HARFIELD: - the process had sort of been - had sort of flowed through the system. Sorry, I
didn't mean to interrupt you, but -
COMMISSIONER: No, no. That's fine. I was interrupting you, really. But it became clear that
the ATO data was being used in an averaged form on these many customers who hadn't
responded. Were they the majority, do you recall?
MS HARFIELD: I don't recall the numbers. I know that certainly sort of across the December
time that there were lots of sort of - we were doing recovery action with individuals who
had - who were complaining. So the letter itself that went out to a customer didn't include
any sort of phone number for a customer to contact. The direction was to go online.
And it emerged through the sort of October, November, December period that as a result of
that, customers were taking to social media to talk about the process itself, and there was
a - you know, an increased dissatisfaction with what was happening in relation to the - so the
process, and people were receiving debt letters but not - having not engaged with the other
elements of the sort of process. And at that point - because there was nowhere to ring, then
those were sort of emerging through that sort of social media-type environment. And so we
were doing recovery action for customers in relation to those issues.
COMMISSIONER: So it was perfectly obvious by that stage, then - this is late 2016 - that the
situation had changed from any concept of ATO data as a last resort?
MS HARFIELD: Yes.

COMMISSIONER: Right. Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Do you have any awareness of testing that was done
prior to the Scheme going fully live in September 2016 as to the number of recipients who
were responding at all to the initial letters notifying the customer of the discrepancy and
asking them to go online?
MS HARFIELD: I don't have the details of that, but I - I mean, I do understand that - I think
Mr Ryman would have been sort of monitoring some of those things, yes.
MR SCOTT: It was quite high, wasn't it?
MS HARFIELD: Yes, it was. In terms of - as I say, through that sort of September, October,
November period, there was definitely an increase in the sort of dissatisfaction from the
customers. And as I say, we also had some systems issues that had correctly - incorrectly
impacted on customers. So we were doing recovery action in relation to individuals, as well
as sort of groups of people in relation to some of the payments, yes.
MR SCOTT: In fact, it was more than half, wasn't it, that recipients who had been sent these
letters in the testing phase that did not respond?
MS HARFIELD: Yes. Yes, I - yes, I believe so.
COMMISSIONER: Well, to be precise, I think the pilot report in August 2015 showed that 60
per cent did not respond.
MR SCOTT: So it was abundantly clear, wasn't it, having regard to the number of customers
who were not going to respond - sorry, who had not responded in the pilot, that under this
Scheme, averaging was going to, by default, become the main methodology for calculating
these recipients' income, wasn't it?
MS HARFIELD: Well, it was certainly going to be the thing that generated the debt, yes.
